extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, physicists, and advanced students studying classical mechanics (Newtonian motion with resistance); readers of Newton's Principia
extracted.subtask_description: Geometrical and analytical methods for determining motion of bodies in a resisting medium (including how to infer the curve described, the medium's resistance/density distribution, and velocities) primarily treating resistance proportional to velocity or to the square of velocity. Includes lemmas on moments (fluxions) and worked examples (circle, parabola, hyperbola).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodus determinandi Curvam DraF ex Phænomenis
rubrics_metrics.description: Method of determining the curve DraF which the same body describes from measured phenomena (landing points) and thereby deducing the medium's resistance and the body's velocities at each place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Project two similar and equal bodies from the same place D with equal velocities but differing angles CDP and cDp, observe impact points F and f on horizontal DC. Assume a trial relation of resistance to gravity (represented by a trial length SM for DP), compute by calculation the resulting DF and Df from the assumed DP and compare the ratio Ff ÷ DF from computation to that found experimentally; the difference is plotted as perpendicular MN. Repeat with different assumed ratios SM, collect positive differences on one side of the line SM and negative on the other, and draw a regular curve NNN cutting the line SMMM in X; SX gives the true ratio of resistance to gravity. From that ratio one deduces the true DP (and thus the curve DraF, velocities and resistances at places).

rubrics_metrics.name: From a given curve derive velocity and resistance at each point
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the curve DraF (the path of the body), one can determine both the body's initial velocity and the medium's resistance at each point r.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the given relation CP×AC to DP×DA one obtains both the initial resistance and the parabola's latus rectum; from the length of the tangent rL one gets the velocity proportional to it, and the resistance in a place r proportional to that velocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of linear vs quadratic resistance hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypothesis that resistance is proportional to velocity is chiefly a mathematical approximation; it holds approximately for bodies moving very slowly in media with some rigidity, whereas in perfectly non-rigid media resistance is proportional to the square of the velocity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the linear-in-velocity law for slow motions or media with some rigidity; for many real media (no rigidity) adopt the quadratic law and derive the resulting motion laws accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. V (Theor. III) — consequences of quadratic resistance with geometrically spaced times
rubrics_metrics.description: If a body's resistance is proportional to the square of its velocity and the sequence of observation times is taken in geometric progression from smaller to larger, then the initial velocities for each time-interval are in the same geometric progression inverted, and the distances described in each of those times are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction/proof uses hyperbola with rectangular asymptotes: if time-parts AK, KL, LM,... correspond to CA, CK, CL,... in geometric progression then the squares of the velocities at each start are proportional to their decrements, leading to the specified relations. Consequence: areas described by those velocity-lines correspond to spaces described, so equal-area pieces correspond to equal spaces per equal time partitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbolic-area representation of motion in quadratic resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: The space described in a resisting medium (resistance ∝ v^2) during a time interval can be represented by a hyperbolic area adjacent to ordinates proportional to velocities and the base representing time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If time is represented by part AD and initial velocity by ordinate AB, the final velocity is given by ordinate DG and the space described equals the hyperbolic area ABGD; ratio comparisons between motion in resisting and non-resisting media are given by ratios of such hyperbolic area to the rectangle AB×AD. Also hyperbolic constructions yield the maximum attainable velocity and relations between resistance and a centripetal force equivalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scaling laws for spherical bodies under quadratic resistance (Prop. VI & corol.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Homogeneous equal spheres under quadratic resistance and acted on only by impressed forces: if times are reciprocals of the initial velocities, they always describe equal spaces and lose parts of their velocities proportional to the whole; scaling laws relate spaces described to diameters and densities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For spheres with equal initial velocities but differing diameters/densities, and resistance ∝ (diameter^2 × velocity^2), one derives that the motion of a sphere is proportional to velocity × mass (velocity × cube of diameter), giving corollaries: if resistance scales as D^n the spaces that retain proportional velocities are ∝ D^{3-n}; if bodies are non-homogeneous, space scales with density; medium differences alter space in inverse proportion to resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal/resistive relation for proportional loss of motion (Prop. VII)
rubrics_metrics.description: If bodies are resisted in the duplicate ratio of velocities, then to lose parts of motion proportional to the whole the times must be directly as the initial motions and inversely as the initial resistances; spaces described during such times are proportional to the product of initial velocities and those times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: lost parts of motion are proportional to resistances × times; setting those losses proportional to the whole motion yields the stated relation among time, resistance and initial motion; consequences for equal-velocity bodies with resistances scaling with diameter powers follow (see corollaries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma II — moments (fluxions) of generated quantities
rubrics_metrics.description: The moment (instantaneous generated increment) of a generated quantity equals the sum of the moments of each generating term, with coefficients given by the term's degree and the fluxion of the base quantities; rules for moments of products, powers, roots, quotients are given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines 'genita' and 'momentum' in algebraic and geometric contexts; gives formulae: moment of A^n is n a A^{n-1}, moment of A^{m/n} is (m/n) a A^{(m-n)/n}, moment of product A^2×B is 2 a A B + A^2 b, etc. Cases and corollaries show how to compute moments in proportional sequences, rectangles, sums/differences of squares, and apply to fluxional calculus (finding maxima/minima, tangents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VIII (Theor. VI) — geometric progression of absolute forces over equal space parts
rubrics_metrics.description: For a body ascending or descending in a uniform medium with uniform gravity, if the total space is divided into equal parts and at the start of each part the absolute force (gravity ± resistance) is collected, then those absolute forces form a geometric progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent gravity by line AC and resistance by AK; velocities by AP (mean proportional of AK and AC). Using hyperbola with rectangular asymptotes one shows infinitesimal area elements KNOL are proportional to AP, so splitting the total hyperbolic area into equal parts yields absolute forces AC, IC, KC, LC,... in geometric progression. Corollaries: one can represent gravity, velocity, and resistance by lines from such an area; the maximum velocity attainable in infinite descent is given by a particular line AC; relations between small time-particles and rectangular products are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. IX (Theor. VII) — times represented by circular and hyperbolic sectors
rubrics_metrics.description: If tangents of the circular sector and of the hyperbolic sector are taken proportional to velocities (with a suitable radius), then the whole future ascent time equals the circular sector and the whole past descent time equals the hyperbolic sector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a circle quadrant and a rectangular-hyperbola with a common perpendicular AD; if the tangents Ap and AP are proportional to velocities, then by slicing into infinitesimal particles and comparing with earlier corollaries one shows sector AtD measures ascent time and hyperbolic sector ATD measures descent time. Corollaries give comparisons between velocities in resisting and non-resisting media by comparing triangular and sector areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. X (Prob. III) — determining medium density and velocity to make a body follow a given curve
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a horizontal plane and a specified curve ACK, with gravity directed uniformly toward the horizon and resistance proportional to medium density × velocity^2, determine the medium density distribution at each place that makes a projectile move exactly along the given curve, and find the body's velocity at each point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider infinitesimal chord arcs and their rectilinear equivalents CH, Ch; tangents at the point give CF and Cf described by the body when progressing or regressing. Using small generated line-elements, resistance ∝ density × (CF^2/FG) and comparing generated line-elements HF and FG yields density ∝ (Cf - CF) ÷ CF^2. Corollaries provide formulae: if CF = CK then one gets explicit density expressions in terms of tangent length and other geometric quantities. The method reduces problems to series expansions of the ordinate if necessary and demonstrates with examples (semicircle, parabola, hyperbola) how to compute the necessary density — e.g., for a semicircle the density comes out proportional to tangent length CT (a/e) and resistance to gravity in a given ratio, while for a parabola no finite medium density will produce motion along that parabola (Galileo's result). Several worked examples show specific algebraic expansions and substitutions to get explicit density laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of series expansion to solve density-for-curve problems (Corollary to Prop. X)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the curve is given by a relation between abscissa and ordinate and the ordinate is resolvable into a convergent series, the problem (finding medium density to produce that curve) can be solved expediently by taking the first terms of the series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish successive series-terms by order in the small parameter; the first term corresponds to the ordinate near the origin, the second to the difference between ordinate and tangent position (determining tangent location), the third to curvature, etc. Truncating after a sufficient number of terms yields approximate expressions for CF, FG±kl and hence for the medium density via the general formula S ÷ {R √(1+QQ)} given in the rule. Examples illustrate this series procedure for circle, parabola, hyperbola.
